Figure 1 adds cross-cutting layers "Data and bias", "Reliability evaluation" and "Discussion and outlook" (p. 3) [V, from figure].
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [A] Traditional methods (SAST, GNNs) are discussed "only in two situations": to motivate structural information for Transformers and as baselines or external tools for LLMs; "this paper does not provide a separate review of traditional detection methods" (p. 4). Section 7.1 nevertheless compares LLMs with DL and SAST qualitatively (pp. 11–12).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Secondary literature; the reference list has 32 entries (pp. 14–16).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [I] No corpus size is stated; we counted 32 references (pp. 14–16), of which roughly a dozen are LLM-based detection studies (Table 1 lists 11 representative methods, pp. 6–7). Several references are themselves reviews/surveys [2–4, 18–21] (pp. 14–15).
- Sampling / selection method: not reported. [I] Reference years run 2019–2026 (pp. 14–16), but no time window is stated. Figure 2 places milestones from 2019 (Devign) to 2026 (context enhancement, M2CVD) (p. 4) [V, from figure].
- Data availability: not applicable / not reported (no extraction sheet or study list released).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: not applicable (no experiments). [V] One quantitative re-analysis: the review re-reads PrimeVul Table V for five code LMs — BigVul train/test F1 62.88%–68.26%, BigVul→PrimeVul F1 1.91%–5.82%, PrimeVul train/test F1 18.05%–21.43%, paired-both-correct 1.06%–3.01% (p. 12). [I] We checked these numbers against the PrimeVul text in this project (ding2025vulnerability, p. 7, Table V); the 68.26%/3.09% pair matches.
- Code availability: not applicable.

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [A] The review recommends reporting at least Precision, Recall, F1 and a confusion matrix, grouped by project, time, language or CWE; Top-k and audit effort at fixed recall for localization; separate checks of location/type/cause/suggestion for explanations; Accuracy only as supplementary; mean, fluctuation range and parse-failure rate for repeated LLM calls (p. 11). It re-reports VD-Score and paired metrics from PrimeVul (p. 11) and Top-10 Accuracy/Effort@20%Recall from LineVul (p. 5).
- Statistical testing: not applicable; the review does no pooling, meta-analysis or effect-size synthesis (not reported).

## 7. Key findings
1. Benchmark inflation — [A] Gains from code pretraining, prompting, fine-tuning and structural enhancement hold "on specific benchmarks" but are "easily affected by duplicate samples, label noise, random splits, temporal leakage, and changes in model versions" (p. 1). Supported by the PrimeVul re-reading: StarCoder2 F1 68.26% on BigVul vs 3.09% on the PrimeVul test set (p. 2) and the five-model ranges above (p. 12).
2. Random-split F1 should be called "within-benchmark performance", not a real-world detection rate; out-of-time testing should be a reliability baseline, combined with project isolation and reporting of time windows, data-freeze dates and model knowledge cutoffs (p. 10) — [A].
3. Contamination from pretraining corpora is treated "as an alternative explanation that needs to be audited", not a confirmed fact; knowledge-cutoff dates are not proof of no contamination (p. 10) — [A].
4. Cross-study ranking is not possible: GRACE, DLAP, context enhancement and M2CVD "all report gains in their own settings, but datasets, model versions, and evaluation protocols differ, so they cannot be directly ranked" (p. 12) — [A]. Table 2 gives a risk matrix (label noise, exact/near duplicates, pretraining contamination, random splitting, cross-project/language failure, class imbalance, false-positive cost, explanation/version validity) with identification signals and mitigations (pp. 10–11) — [V, table content].
5. LLM vs SAST vs DL — [A] "SAST is usually more stable within the scope covered by existing rules, whereas LLMs are better at semantic summarization and alert explanation"; unified benchmarks "support complementarity rather than complete replacement", with the two tool types finding different vulnerabilities and different false positives (p. 12), citing a SAST study [1] and the Gnieciak & Szandala LLM-vs-SAST benchmark [15] (p. 15). No numbers for this comparison are given.
6. Hybrids — [A] Proposed workflow: "SAST candidate generation-LLM review or explanation-human confirmation" (p. 8), to be judged by audit time, false-negative control and explanation consistency rather than overall F1 (p. 8); outputs should not be "simply concatenate[d]" (p. 13). Evidence cited is GRACE (structure + ICL, ≥28.65% relative F1 gain over six baselines, p. 8), DLAP (DL-augmented prompting, p. 8) and the context-enhancement study [29] (p. 8). No quantitative evidence on SAST+LLM hybrids is reported.
7. Cost — [A] API calls, GPU memory, latency, model updates and prompt maintenance should be counted; sensitive code and local large-scale scanning suit lightweight models or SAST; high-risk scenarios should use hybrid workflows with human confirmation (p. 12). No cost figures are reported.
8. Re-reported primary numbers (all [A], from cited papers): LineVul 188k+ functions, F1 +160%–379% over baselines, Top-10 Accuracy +12%–25%, Effort@20%Recall −29%–53% (p. 5); DiverseVul 7,514 commits, 18,945 vulnerable / 330,492 non-vulnerable functions, 150 CWEs (p. 9); LLMVulExp average F1 92.4% on SeVC single-type setting (p. 8).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] No separate limitations section. Scope exclusions: network intrusion, malware, smart contracts, generation, repair (p. 1).
- [A] Traditional detection methods are not reviewed separately (p. 4).
- [A] Specific caveats on cited evidence: the PrimeVul conclusion "is limited to the five models and three settings in Table V" (p. 12); LLMVulExp results "cannot be directly generalized to PrimeVul, cross-project testing, or real deployment" (pp. 8–9); GRACE gain is relative and applies only to the tested configurations (p. 8).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Not systematic: no search protocol, databases, screening, corpus count or quality assessment (absence across pp. 1–4). Its conclusions cannot be checked for selection bias, and it cannot be cited as a systematic review.
- [I] Small and selective corpus (32 references, pp. 14–16). Missing, among others, project-scale LLM/SAST studies and LLM-based SAST-alarm filtering work that we have (e.g. li2026llm, du2026reducing, xiong2026sifting, li2024iris, guo2025repoaudit); hybrid claims rest on GRACE, DLAP and one context-enhancement study (p. 8), not on SAST+LLM evaluations.
- [I] SAST is explicitly out of scope (p. 4), yet the review draws an LLM-vs-SAST conclusion (p. 12) from two references [1, 15] with no numbers. That conclusion is under-supported.
- [I] Contradictions are explained only in general terms. Apart from the PrimeVul Table V re-reading (p. 12), it does not tabulate conflicting results from different studies side by side against their evaluation setups (benchmark, split, class ratio, granularity). Table 1 (pp. 6–7) is qualitative: no numbers, no split type per study.
- [I] Cites PrimeVul as a 2024 arXiv preprint (p. 15) and leans heavily on that one study for the inflation argument.
- [I] Editorial inconsistencies (three vs four RQs, undefined "C2", p. 2, p. 4, p. 12) suggest light editorial review (see Analyst notes on venue).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (selection): [I] Unknown selection process, so selection bias cannot be judged; the reviewer's framing (evaluation pitfalls) may have driven which studies were cited.
- External: [I] Mostly C/C++ function-level benchmarks (BigVul, PrimeVul, DiverseVul, SeVC, ReVeal, FFmpeg+Qemu; pp. 8–9, 12); multilingual evidence is one reference [32] (p. 13).
- Construct: [I] Good conceptual separation of label correctness, localization and explanation evidence (p. 4); recommends metrics beyond F1 (p. 11).
- Statistical conclusion: [I] No quantitative synthesis; confidence levels ("medium confidence to C2", p. 12) are given without a stated grading scheme.
- Reproducibility: [I] Not reproducible as a review (no protocol, no study list beyond references).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: traceable data pipelines with commit, time, label-source and duplicate statistics and updateable data cards (p. 13); out-of-time and project-isolated testing as main evidence, random splits only for historical comparison (p. 13); uncertainty calibration, risk-coverage curves and recall at a fixed false-positive budget (p. 13); decomposed verification of explanations (location, trigger, path, CWE, fix) (p. 13); human-machine studies recording audit time per real vulnerability (p. 13); SAST-LLM systems that measure candidate recall, LLM filtering gain, explanation correctness and total audit cost separately (p. 13); preserving system prompts, model IDs, call dates, temperatures and repetition counts (p. 13).
- Suggested by us [I]: a systematic, protocol-based review that puts SAST, DL and LLM results on the same evaluation-setup axes. This is exactly the gap between this review and ours.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (primary), RQ3 (conceptual only), RQ1 (qualitative only), RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]: This is the closest competing review and must be cited for positioning. Overlap: evaluation-reliability framing (duplicates, label noise, temporal splits, contamination) and the SAST-LLM-human workflow recommendation. Difference: it is narrative, has a small corpus (32 references), explicitly excludes SAST as a reviewed family, gives no quantitative LLM-vs-SAST or hybrid evidence, and does not map contradictions study-by-study onto evaluation setup. Our contribution should be stated against those four points. Its recommendations corroborate our RQ2 answer independently, but at weak strength.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ2 | Benchmark gains are inflated by duplicates, label noise, random splits, temporal leakage and model-version changes; random-split F1 = "within-benchmark performance" only | 1, 10 | A | weak (narrative review) |
| RQ2 | Re-reads PrimeVul Table V: five code LMs F1 62.88–68.26% on BigVul vs 1.91–5.82% BigVul→PrimeVul vs 18.05–21.43% PrimeVul→PrimeVul | 12 | A | moderate (secondary report of a single primary study; numbers match ding2025vulnerability) |
| RQ2 | LLM methods (GRACE, DLAP, context enhancement, M2CVD) cannot be ranked because datasets, model versions and protocols differ | 12 | A | weak |
| RQ1 | SAST more stable within rule coverage; LLMs better at semantic summarisation/explanation; unified benchmarks support complementarity, not replacement (no numbers) | 12 | A | weak |
| RQ3 | Recommends SAST candidates → LLM ranking/explanation → human confirmation; judge by audit time, false negatives, explanation consistency, not F1 | 8, 13 | A | weak (no quantitative hybrid evidence) |
| RQ3 | Costs (API calls, GPU memory, latency, version drift, prompt maintenance) should be reported; none quantified | 9, 12 | A | weak |
| RQ5 | Open problems: out-of-time + project-isolated testing, data cards, uncertainty calibration, fixed-FP-budget recall, explanation verification, audit-time studies | 13 | A | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "this paper does not provide a separate review of traditional detection methods" (p. 4)

> "Existing evidence from unified benchmarks supports complementarity rather than complete replacement by one tool" (p. 12)

> "F1 obtained from a random split should be called “within-benchmark performance” and cannot be directly described as a “real-world detection rate”" (p. 10)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: all 16 PDF pages read in full, including references, funding and copyright notes (pp. 14–16). Figures 1–2 (pp. 3–4) read from the PDF images because pdftotext dropped them.
- Venue quality [I]: Computers and Artificial Intelligence, Vol. 3 No. 5 (2026), E-ISSN 3006-3728, published by "Zeus Press" (p. 1). The PDF has no received/revised/accepted dates and no editor or peer-review statement (pp. 1–16). OpenAlex (queried 2026-11-12) lists the source with no host organisation, `is_in_doaj: false`, `is_core: false`, no indexing lists, and publication date 2026-10-29; cited_by 0 in metadata. The acknowledgment reads only "This paper is an output of the science project." (p. 16). There is a single author, and internal inconsistencies (three vs four RQs; undefined "C2") remain. Together these are warning signs of a low-visibility venue with uncertain peer review. We did not confirm that it is predatory. Treat it as tier 1 by `venue_kind` but weight it like grey literature. Cite it for positioning, not as evidence.
- Competitor positioning [I]: SAST tools are covered only as baselines/external tools, not reviewed (p. 4). Hybrids are covered conceptually (pp. 8, 13), with no SAST+LLM empirical studies. Cross-study contradictions are explained via evaluation setup in general terms and through one worked example (PrimeVul, p. 12), not systematically.
- Uncertainties: whether a systematic search was done but simply not reported. Numbers it gives for other papers are labelled [A] here; only the PrimeVul numbers were cross-checked against a primary text.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Test whether DL vulnerability detectors and LLMs that score well on curated benchmarks still work under deployment-like conditions. The study looks at three things: separability of code representations, within- vs cross-dataset generalisation, and detection of recent, temporally separated vulnerabilities (p. 1, p. 2).
- [A] Contribution claimed: VentiVul, a temporally separated out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmark of 200 CVEs / 263 vulnerable–patched pairs, plus a "Whole-File" + "Function-Pair" evaluation protocol (p. 2). "Out-of-distribution" means test data drawn from a different source or period than the training data.

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] RQ1: do graph-based and CodeBERT representations separate vulnerable from non-vulnerable code before task-specific training? (p. 6)
- [A] RQ2: how do benchmark characteristics affect within-dataset and cross-dataset performance of DL detectors? (p. 7)
- [A] RQ3: how well do trained DL models and off-the-shelf LLMs detect recent vulnerabilities on a temporally separated benchmark? (p. 7)
- No formal hypotheses.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Controlled empirical evaluation in three stages: representation diagnostics (t-SNE + centroid distance), 4×4 train/test matrix of DL models across datasets, inference-only evaluation on VentiVul (pp. 6–8).
- Approach / models: [V] DL: Devign (gated GNN on code property graphs), ReVeal (Joern graphs + token embeddings, SMOTE), LineVul (fine-tuned CodeBERT), VulBERTa (RoBERTa pretrained on C/C++) (p. 5). LLMs, open-weight, no fine-tuning: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct (16B MoE, 2.4B active), Qwen3-30B-A3B (thinking mode disabled), Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501, all released before May 2025 (p. 5, p. 8).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] DL vs LLM only on VentiVul. Only ReVeal and LineVul (each trained on the four datasets) were taken to VentiVul; Devign and VulBERTa were not (p. 7). LLM prompting: zero-shot, few-shot (k=4, two complete pairs), chain-of-thought (p. 8, Table 4 p. 9). [I] No SAST tool, no proprietary/frontier LLM, no fine-tuned LLM and no trivial baseline (e.g. all-positive or random) is included.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Juliet 253,002 functions, 37% vulnerable, synthetic; Devign 27,318, 46%, manual; BigVul 188,636, 6%, patches; ICVul 15,396, 41%, patches (p. 3, Table 1). All C/C++.
- VentiVul: [V] CVEs for Linux and Chromium disclosed from May 1, 2025, taken from NVD in disclosure order until 100 per project; manually verified; target size fixed before collection; "records were not selected based on model predictions" (p. 4). 13,326 functions, 200 CVEs, 39 CWEs, 263 pairs; Chromium 7,095 functions / 100 CVEs / 20 CWEs / 147 pairs; Linux 6,231 / 100 / 27 / 116 (p. 4, Table 2). Pre-fix function = vulnerable, post-fix = non-vulnerable, plus other functions from the same files labelled non-vulnerable to keep realistic imbalance (p. 4).
- Sample size (N) and unit: functions (Whole-File), CVEs (CDR) and vulnerable–patched pairs (PACC) (p. 7). [I] With 263 vulnerable functions in 13,326, VentiVul prevalence is about 2.0%. We infer this from p. 4; the paper does not state the positive count for Whole-File.
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Inclusion: valid references, explicit fix in non-test C/C++ files, CWE available; excluded: missing references, non-C/C++ or test-only fixes, fixes with "excessive unrelated files or functions" (p. 4). Train/test split ratios for the four benchmarks: not reported.
- Data availability: [V] "All of our datasets, code, and results are available" on GitHub (p. 2).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] DL models use the original authors' code and "recommended settings" (p. 8); H100 GPUs (p. 8). Leakage controls: strict train–test splits with duplicate functions filtered, a fixed test set per target benchmark (p. 7). LLMs run locally via vLLM on B200 GPUs, temperature 0, top-p 1, seed 42, max 384 output tokens, JSON-only binary label; unparseable outputs kept as failures (p. 8). Each model, DL or LLM, receives one function at a time (p. 7, p. 8). Few-shot demonstrations are removed from the test set by pair identifier and code hash (p. 8). ReVeal metrics are computed only over functions its preprocessing can handle (p. 7). Two policies for LLMs: valid-only and conservative (failures counted wrong) (p. 8).
- Code availability: [V] public GitHub repository (p. 2).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 for Whole-File (p. 9). CVE Detection Rate (CDR): share of CVEs with at least one vulnerable function flagged, i.e. CVE-level coverage (p. 9). Patch Pair Accuracy (PACC): share of pairs where the vulnerable version is flagged and the patched version is not, i.e. sensitivity to the fix (p. 9). Centroid distance in min-max normalised t-SNE space, described as descriptive only (pp. 8–9).
- Statistical testing: not reported. There are no significance tests, confidence intervals or repeated runs; LLMs use one deterministic run (p. 8) and DL results come from single training runs (seeds for DL not reported).

## 7. Key findings
1. In-distribution DL (within-dataset) — [V] LineVul F1 94.52 and VulBERTa 94.14 on Juliet; LineVul F1 91.00 on BigVul (p. 11; Table 6 p. 12). On BigVul, ReVeal, Devign and VulBERTa reach accuracy 87.45, 94.09, 94.39 but F1 only 23.58, 16.90, 0.19 (p. 11). Accuracy is therefore misleading at 6% prevalence.
2. Cross-dataset DL — [V] LineVul (Juliet) F1 94.52 in-dataset falls to 53.95 (Devign), 10.73 (BigVul), 51.22 (ICVul) (p. 11). LineVul (BigVul) falls from 91.00 to 0 (Juliet), 1.90 (Devign), 13.05 (ICVul) (p. 12). ReVeal (BigVul) is below 1.00 F1 on all three external sets (p. 11). [A] "No evaluated model consistently preserves its within-dataset performance" (p. 11).
3. Temporally separated DL (VentiVul, Whole-File) — [V] F1 3.47–8.65 across the 8 ReVeal/LineVul configurations; best ReVeal (BigVul) F1 8.65 with precision 5.25%, recall 24.43% (p. 13, Table 7). Devign-trained models: recall 99.24–100% but precision about 2% (p. 13, Table 7). LineVul (BigVul) F1 6.87 on VentiVul vs 91.00 in-distribution (Table 7 p. 13; Table 6 p. 12).
4. Temporally separated LLMs (VentiVul) — [V] Conservative F1 0.79–5.36 across 4 models × 3 prompts; all conservative F1 < 5.5% and all PACC < 6% (p. 13; Table 8 p. 14). Best: Mistral-Small-24B few-shot F1 5.36%, CDR 46%, PACC 5.75% (p. 13). Highest valid-only F1: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B CoT 8.21% (conservative 3.04%) (p. 14, Table 8). Zero-shot conservative F1: Qwen2.5-Coder 3.72, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite 4.29, Qwen3 3.09, Mistral 4.07 (p. 14, Table 8). LLM precision and recall are not reported, and the LLMs have no in-distribution numbers.
5. DL vs LLM on the same OOD data [V/I] — best DL F1 8.65 (ReVeal-BigVul) vs best LLM conservative F1 5.36 (Mistral few-shot) (p. 13; p. 14). Zero-shot LLM CDR (34%, 20%, 9%, 5%) is lower than most DL configurations (p. 13). Best PACC: DL 5.34% vs LLM 5.75% (p. 13). [I] Both families are close to an all-positive predictor at ~2% prevalence (F1 ≈ 3.9%, our calculation from p. 4 counts); LineVul (Devign) at recall 100%, precision 2%, F1 3.93 is effectively that predictor (p. 13, Table 7).
6. CDR vs PACC gap — [V] ReVeal (Devign), ReVeal (ICVul), LineVul (Devign) reach CDR 99.10%, 94.59%, 100% but PACC 0.76%, 0%, 0% (p. 13). [A] Detecting a vulnerable function "does not imply" telling it apart from its patch (p. 13).
7. Prompting — [V] Few-shot improves Mistral on all three metrics but degrades the other models; CoT raises Qwen2.5-Coder valid-only F1 but lowers its PACC (p. 13). [A] Prompting effects are "model- and metric-dependent" (p. 13).
8. Project/CWE variation — [V] All LLMs have higher CDR on Linux than Chromium. DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite zero-shot CDR is 26% on Chromium and 42% on Linux (p. 13). LineVul (BigVul) has CDR 76% on Chromium and 0 on Linux (p. 13). Best project-specific PACC is < 8% (LineVul-ICVul 7.48% on Chromium) (p. 14). Per-CWE PACC peaks at 18.18% (LineVul-ICVul, CWE-472) on small cells (p. 14).
9. Representations — [V] GNN centroid distances: Juliet 0.0242, ICVul 0.0057, BigVul 0.1612; CodeBERT: BigVul 0.166, Devign 0.0068 (pp. 9–10). [A] Neither representation consistently separates vulnerable from non-vulnerable code (p. 10).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Only four DL models, two DL families on VentiVul, four open-weight LLMs; no proprietary LLMs; conclusions apply to the evaluated models (p. 17).
- [A] LLM pretraining corpora and cutoffs are unknown, so temporal separation "cannot fully exclude training-data contamination" (p. 17).
- [A] t-SNE is parameter-sensitive, and centroid distance cannot capture nonlinear structure. RQ1 does not establish a causal link to RQ2/RQ3 performance (p. 17, p. 15).
- [A] Dataset characteristics vary simultaneously, so individual causes cannot be isolated. Preprocessing drops some functions, which affects comparability (p. 17).

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Test whether DL vulnerability detectors and LLMs that score well on curated benchmarks still work under deployment-like conditions. The study looks at three things: separability of code representations, within- vs cross-dataset generalisation, and detection of recent, temporally separated vulnerabilities (p. 1, p. 2).
- [A] Contribution claimed: VentiVul, a temporally separated out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmark of 200 CVEs / 263 vulnerable–patched pairs, plus a "Whole-File" + "Function-Pair" evaluation protocol (p. 2). "Out-of-distribution" means test data drawn from a different source or period than the training data.

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] RQ1: do graph-based and CodeBERT representations separate vulnerable from non-vulnerable code before task-specific training? (p. 6)
- [A] RQ2: how do benchmark characteristics affect within-dataset and cross-dataset performance of DL detectors? (p. 7)
- [A] RQ3: how well do trained DL models and off-the-shelf LLMs detect recent vulnerabilities on a temporally separated benchmark? (p. 7)
- No formal hypotheses.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Controlled empirical evaluation in three stages: representation diagnostics (t-SNE + centroid distance), 4×4 train/test matrix of DL models across datasets, inference-only evaluation on VentiVul (pp. 6–8).
- Approach / models: [V] DL: Devign (gated GNN on code property graphs), ReVeal (Joern graphs + token embeddings, SMOTE), LineVul (fine-tuned CodeBERT), VulBERTa (RoBERTa pretrained on C/C++) (p. 5). LLMs, open-weight, no fine-tuning: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct (16B MoE, 2.4B active), Qwen3-30B-A3B (thinking mode disabled), Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501, all released before May 2025 (p. 5, p. 8).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] DL vs LLM only on VentiVul. Only ReVeal and LineVul (each trained on the four datasets) were taken to VentiVul; Devign and VulBERTa were not (p. 7). LLM prompting: zero-shot, few-shot (k=4, two complete pairs), chain-of-thought (p. 8, Table 4 p. 9). [I] No SAST tool, no proprietary/frontier LLM, no fine-tuned LLM and no trivial baseline (e.g. all-positive or random) is included.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Juliet 253,002 functions, 37% vulnerable, synthetic; Devign 27,318, 46%, manual; BigVul 188,636, 6%, patches; ICVul 15,396, 41%, patches (p. 3, Table 1). All C/C++.
- VentiVul: [V] CVEs for Linux and Chromium disclosed from May 1, 2025, taken from NVD in disclosure order until 100 per project; manually verified; target size fixed before collection; "records were not selected based on model predictions" (p. 4). 13,326 functions, 200 CVEs, 39 CWEs, 263 pairs; Chromium 7,095 functions / 100 CVEs / 20 CWEs / 147 pairs; Linux 6,231 / 100 / 27 / 116 (p. 4, Table 2). Pre-fix function = vulnerable, post-fix = non-vulnerable, plus other functions from the same files labelled non-vulnerable to keep realistic imbalance (p. 4).
- Sample size (N) and unit: functions (Whole-File), CVEs (CDR) and vulnerable–patched pairs (PACC) (p. 7). [I] With 263 vulnerable functions in 13,326, VentiVul prevalence is about 2.0%. We infer this from p. 4; the paper does not state the positive count for Whole-File.
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Inclusion: valid references, explicit fix in non-test C/C++ files, CWE available; excluded: missing references, non-C/C++ or test-only fixes, fixes with "excessive unrelated files or functions" (p. 4). Train/test split ratios for the four benchmarks: not reported.
- Data availability: [V] "All of our datasets, code, and results are available" on GitHub (p. 2).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] DL models use the original authors' code and "recommended settings" (p. 8); H100 GPUs (p. 8). Leakage controls: strict train–test splits with duplicate functions filtered, a fixed test set per target benchmark (p. 7). LLMs run locally via vLLM on B200 GPUs, temperature 0, top-p 1, seed 42, max 384 output tokens, JSON-only binary label; unparseable outputs kept as failures (p. 8). Each model, DL or LLM, receives one function at a time (p. 7, p. 8). Few-shot demonstrations are removed from the test set by pair identifier and code hash (p. 8). ReVeal metrics are computed only over functions its preprocessing can handle (p. 7). Two policies for LLMs: valid-only and conservative (failures counted wrong) (p. 8).
- Code availability: [V] public GitHub repository (p. 2).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 for Whole-File (p. 9). CVE Detection Rate (CDR): share of CVEs with at least one vulnerable function flagged, i.e. CVE-level coverage (p. 9). Patch Pair Accuracy (PACC): share of pairs where the vulnerable version is flagged and the patched version is not, i.e. sensitivity to the fix (p. 9). Centroid distance in min-max normalised t-SNE space, described as descriptive only (pp. 8–9).
- Statistical testing: not reported. There are no significance tests, confidence intervals or repeated runs; LLMs use one deterministic run (p. 8) and DL results come from single training runs (seeds for DL not reported).

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Test whether DL vulnerability detectors and LLMs that score well on curated benchmarks still work under deployment-like conditions. The study looks at three things: separability of code representations, within- vs cross-dataset generalisation, and detection of recent, temporally separated vulnerabilities (p. 1, p. 2).
- [A] Contribution claimed: VentiVul, a temporally separated out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmark of 200 CVEs / 263 vulnerable–patched pairs, plus a "Whole-File" + "Function-Pair" evaluation protocol (p. 2). "Out-of-distribution" means test data drawn from a different source or period than the training data.

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] RQ1: do graph-based and CodeBERT representations separate vulnerable from non-vulnerable code before task-specific training? (p. 6)
- [A] RQ2: how do benchmark characteristics affect within-dataset and cross-dataset performance of DL detectors? (p. 7)
- [A] RQ3: how well do trained DL models and off-the-shelf LLMs detect recent vulnerabilities on a temporally separated benchmark? (p. 7)
- No formal hypotheses.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Controlled empirical evaluation in three stages: representation diagnostics (t-SNE + centroid distance), 4×4 train/test matrix of DL models across datasets, inference-only evaluation on VentiVul (pp. 6–8).
- Approach / models: [V] DL: Devign (gated GNN on code property graphs), ReVeal (Joern graphs + token embeddings, SMOTE), LineVul (fine-tuned CodeBERT), VulBERTa (RoBERTa pretrained on C/C++) (p. 5). LLMs, open-weight, no fine-tuning: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct (16B MoE, 2.4B active), Qwen3-30B-A3B (thinking mode disabled), Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501, all released before May 2025 (p. 5, p. 8).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] DL vs LLM only on VentiVul. Only ReVeal and LineVul (each trained on the four datasets) were taken to VentiVul; Devign and VulBERTa were not (p. 7). LLM prompting: zero-shot, few-shot (k=4, two complete pairs), chain-of-thought (p. 8, Table 4 p. 9). [I] No SAST tool, no proprietary/frontier LLM, no fine-tuned LLM and no trivial baseline (e.g. all-positive or random) is included.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] Juliet 253,002 functions, 37% vulnerable, synthetic; Devign 27,318, 46%, manual; BigVul 188,636, 6%, patches; ICVul 15,396, 41%, patches (p. 3, Table 1). All C/C++.
- VentiVul: [V] CVEs for Linux and Chromium disclosed from May 1, 2025, taken from NVD in disclosure order until 100 per project; manually verified; target size fixed before collection; "records were not selected based on model predictions" (p. 4). 13,326 functions, 200 CVEs, 39 CWEs, 263 pairs; Chromium 7,095 functions / 100 CVEs / 20 CWEs / 147 pairs; Linux 6,231 / 100 / 27 / 116 (p. 4, Table 2). Pre-fix function = vulnerable, post-fix = non-vulnerable, plus other functions from the same files labelled non-vulnerable to keep realistic imbalance (p. 4).
- Sample size (N) and unit: functions (Whole-File), CVEs (CDR) and vulnerable–patched pairs (PACC) (p. 7). [I] With 263 vulnerable functions in 13,326, VentiVul prevalence is about 2.0%. We infer this from p. 4; the paper does not state the positive count for Whole-File.
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Inclusion: valid references, explicit fix in non-test C/C++ files, CWE available; excluded: missing references, non-C/C++ or test-only fixes, fixes with "excessive unrelated files or functions" (p. 4). Train/test split ratios for the four benchmarks: not reported.
- Data availability: [V] "All of our datasets, code, and results are available" on GitHub (p. 2).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] DL models use the original authors' code and "recommended settings" (p. 8); H100 GPUs (p. 8). Leakage controls: strict train–test splits with duplicate functions filtered, a fixed test set per target benchmark (p. 7). LLMs run locally via vLLM on B200 GPUs, temperature 0, top-p 1, seed 42, max 384 output tokens, JSON-only binary label; unparseable outputs kept as failures (p. 8). Each model, DL or LLM, receives one function at a time (p. 7, p. 8). Few-shot demonstrations are removed from the test set by pair identifier and code hash (p. 8). ReVeal metrics are computed only over functions its preprocessing can handle (p. 7). Two policies for LLMs: valid-only and conservative (failures counted wrong) (p. 8).
- Code availability: [V] public GitHub repository (p. 2).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 for Whole-File (p. 9). CVE Detection Rate (CDR): share of CVEs with at least one vulnerable function flagged, i.e. CVE-level coverage (p. 9). Patch Pair Accuracy (PACC): share of pairs where the vulnerable version is flagged and the patched version is not, i.e. sensitivity to the fix (p. 9). Centroid distance in min-max normalised t-SNE space, described as descriptive only (pp. 8–9).
- Statistical testing: not reported. There are no significance tests, confidence intervals or repeated runs; LLMs use one deterministic run (p. 8) and DL results come from single training runs (seeds for DL not reported).

## 7. Key findings
1. In-distribution DL (within-dataset) — [V] LineVul F1 94.52 and VulBERTa 94.14 on Juliet; LineVul F1 91.00 on BigVul (p. 11; Table 6 p. 12). On BigVul, ReVeal, Devign and VulBERTa reach accuracy 87.45, 94.09, 94.39 but F1 only 23.58, 16.90, 0.19 (p. 11). Accuracy is therefore misleading at 6% prevalence.
2. Cross-dataset DL — [V] LineVul (Juliet) F1 94.52 in-dataset falls to 53.95 (Devign), 10.73 (BigVul), 51.22 (ICVul) (p. 11). LineVul (BigVul) falls from 91.00 to 0 (Juliet), 1.90 (Devign), 13.05 (ICVul) (p. 12). ReVeal (BigVul) is below 1.00 F1 on all three external sets (p. 11). [A] "No evaluated model consistently preserves its within-dataset performance" (p. 11).
3. Temporally separated DL (VentiVul, Whole-File) — [V] F1 3.47–8.65 across the 8 ReVeal/LineVul configurations; best ReVeal (BigVul) F1 8.65 with precision 5.25%, recall 24.43% (p. 13, Table 7). Devign-trained models: recall 99.24–100% but precision about 2% (p. 13, Table 7). LineVul (BigVul) F1 6.87 on VentiVul vs 91.00 in-distribution (Table 7 p. 13; Table 6 p. 12).
4. Temporally separated LLMs (VentiVul) — [V] Conservative F1 0.79–5.36 across 4 models × 3 prompts; all conservative F1 < 5.5% and all PACC < 6% (p. 13; Table 8 p. 14). Best: Mistral-Small-24B few-shot F1 5.36%, CDR 46%, PACC 5.75% (p. 13). Highest valid-only F1: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B CoT 8.21% (conservative 3.04%) (p. 14, Table 8). Zero-shot conservative F1: Qwen2.5-Coder 3.72, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite 4.29, Qwen3 3.09, Mistral 4.07 (p. 14, Table 8). LLM precision and recall are not reported, and the LLMs have no in-distribution numbers.
5. DL vs LLM on the same OOD data [V/I] — best DL F1 8.65 (ReVeal-BigVul) vs best LLM conservative F1 5.36 (Mistral few-shot) (p. 13; p. 14). Zero-shot LLM CDR (34%, 20%, 9%, 5%) is lower than most DL configurations (p. 13). Best PACC: DL 5.34% vs LLM 5.75% (p. 13). [I] Both families are close to an all-positive predictor at ~2% prevalence (F1 ≈ 3.9%, our calculation from p. 4 counts); LineVul (Devign) at recall 100%, precision 2%, F1 3.93 is effectively that predictor (p. 13, Table 7).
6. CDR vs PACC gap — [V] ReVeal (Devign), ReVeal (ICVul), LineVul (Devign) reach CDR 99.10%, 94.59%, 100% but PACC 0.76%, 0%, 0% (p. 13). [A] Detecting a vulnerable function "does not imply" telling it apart from its patch (p. 13).
7. Prompting — [V] Few-shot improves Mistral on all three metrics but degrades the other models; CoT raises Qwen2.5-Coder valid-only F1 but lowers its PACC (p. 13). [A] Prompting effects are "model- and metric-dependent" (p. 13).
8. Project/CWE variation — [V] All LLMs have higher CDR on Linux than Chromium. DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite zero-shot CDR is 26% on Chromium and 42% on Linux (p. 13). LineVul (BigVul) has CDR 76% on Chromium and 0 on Linux (p. 13). Best project-specific PACC is < 8% (LineVul-ICVul 7.48% on Chromium) (p. 14). Per-CWE PACC peaks at 18.18% (LineVul-ICVul, CWE-472) on small cells (p. 14).
9. Representations — [V] GNN centroid distances: Juliet 0.0242, ICVul 0.0057, BigVul 0.1612; CodeBERT: BigVul 0.166, Devign 0.0068 (pp. 9–10). [A] Neither representation consistently separates vulnerable from non-vulnerable code (p. 10).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Only four DL models, two DL families on VentiVul, four open-weight LLMs; no proprietary LLMs; conclusions apply to the evaluated models (p. 17).
- [A] LLM pretraining corpora and cutoffs are unknown, so temporal separation "cannot fully exclude training-data contamination" (p. 17).
- [A] t-SNE is parameter-sensitive, and centroid distance cannot capture nonlinear structure. RQ1 does not establish a causal link to RQ2/RQ3 performance (p. 17, p. 15).
- [A] Dataset characteristics vary simultaneously, so individual causes cannot be isolated. Preprocessing drops some functions, which affects comparability (p. 17).
- [A] VentiVul is C/C++ only (Linux, Chromium) and may not generalise to other languages or proprietary code. "Unrelated" functions may hide other vulnerabilities (residual label noise), and regex function extraction can miss complex C/C++ syntax, which mainly affects Whole-File (p. 17).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] No trivial baseline. At ~2% prevalence an all-positive classifier scores F1 ≈ 3.9%, so most reported DL and LLM F1 values (3.09–8.65) are at or barely above chance. The paper describes them as "low" but never compares them with chance.
- [I] The DL and LLM comparison is asymmetric. DL models were trained on historical data; LLMs were used zero/few-shot without fine-tuning, with small open-weight models (MoE models with 2.4–3B active parameters) and Qwen3 thinking disabled (p. 5, p. 8). The study says nothing about frontier or fine-tuned LLMs, and nothing about LLMs in-distribution, because LLMs were not run on the four benchmarks.
- [I] LLM precision/recall are not reported (Table 8 gives F1, CDR, PACC only, p. 14), so we cannot tell whether LLMs fail through false positives or false negatives.
- [I] Single run, no confidence intervals; with 263 pairs, PACC differences of a few points (e.g. 5.34% vs 5.75%) are within noise.
- [I] One function at a time with no context (p. 7). This is fair between families but disadvantages LLMs, which may need inter-procedural context. Many Linux/Chromium bugs need cross-function reasoning (cf. CVE-2025-37777 spanning two files, p. 4).
- [I] No static-analysis tool is evaluated, although the introduction positions learning-based detection as a complement to static analysis (p. 1).
- [I] Preprint status: arXiv v4 dated 4 Nov 2026 carries a footnote "accepted for publication in the Journal of Systems and Software" (p. 1). Acceptance is author-stated; no journal DOI is in metadata.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal: [I] Deduplication within datasets and fixed test sets are reported (p. 7), but split ratios and cross-dataset overlap checks (e.g. Devign/BigVul share FFmpeg/QEMU-type C projects) are not reported. ReVeal is scored only on functions it can process (p. 7), which may inflate or deflate its numbers relative to LineVul.
- External: [I] C/C++, two very large projects, 200 CVEs, open-weight mid-size LLMs only (p. 4, p. 5).
- Construct: [I] Labelling unrelated same-file functions as non-vulnerable (p. 4) is a realistic construct for "scan the whole file", though label noise remains (p. 17). PACC is a strict and useful measure of patch sensitivity. CDR rewards indiscriminate positive prediction, as the paper itself shows (p. 13).
- Statistical conclusion: [I] No tests, single runs, small per-CWE cells (p. 14).
- Reproducibility: [I] Good: data, code and results are public (p. 2), and decoding settings and prompts are fully given (p. 8, p. 9). DL hyper-parameters are given only by reference to the original implementations (p. 8).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: representations and training that emphasise security-relevant changes, e.g. vulnerable–patched pair supervision (p. 16); datasets prioritising reliable labels, diverse patterns and explicit vulnerability–fix links over size (p. 16); complementing within-dataset evaluation with cross-dataset and temporally separated testing, and reporting CDR and patch-pair metrics with function-level metrics (p. 16); studying individual dataset factors, broader ecosystems and "more advanced LLM adaptation strategies" (p. 16).
- Suggested by us [I]: run SAST tools and frontier/fine-tuned LLMs on VentiVul with file/repository context and a chance baseline. That would give exactly the same-benchmark LLM vs SAST vs DL comparison our RQ5 identifies as missing.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (DL vs LLM on same OOD data), RQ2 (temporal separation, cross-dataset shift, class ratio, accuracy vs F1), RQ4 (per-project and per-CWE variation, C/C++), RQ5 (patch-pair sensitivity, chance baselines).
- How it informs our work [I]: This is the strongest direct evidence in our set that in-distribution DL scores (F1 91–94.5) do not survive temporal and dataset shift (F1 3.5–8.7). Off-the-shelf mid-size LLMs do no better than the shifted DL detectors, and both sit near chance. It supports the RQ2 claim that evaluation setup drives the reported ranking, and agrees with the PrimeVul near-random pair results (ding2025vulnerability). It covers no SAST tool or cost, so it adds nothing for RQ3.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ2 | In-distribution DL F1 is high (LineVul 94.52 Juliet, 91.00 BigVul; VulBERTa 94.14 Juliet) but drops cross-dataset (LineVul-BigVul → 0 / 1.90 / 13.05; LineVul-Juliet → 53.95 / 10.73 / 51.22) | 11, 12 | V | moderate (preprint, single run, 4 models) |
| RQ2 | High accuracy hides failure at 6% prevalence: BigVul accuracy 87.45/94.09/94.39 with F1 23.58/16.90/0.19 (ReVeal/Devign/VulBERTa) | 11 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | On temporally separated VentiVul (CVEs from May 2025, ~2% prevalence), trained DL F1 3.47–8.65 (best ReVeal-BigVul 8.65, P 5.25%) | 13 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | On the same VentiVul functions, 4 open-weight LLMs (zero/few-shot/CoT) reach conservative F1 0.79–5.36 (best Mistral-24B few-shot), PACC < 6%; zero-shot CDR 5–34%, below most DL configs | 13, 14 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | Both families are close to an all-positive baseline (F1 ≈ 3.9% at ~2% prevalence); no family is practically usable on recent CVEs | 4, 13 | I | moderate (our calculation from reported counts) |
| RQ2 | High CVE-level coverage does not mean patch sensitivity: CDR 94.59–100% with PACC 0–0.76% for Devign/ICVul-trained models; all DL PACC < 5.5% | 13 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | Results vary by project and CWE: LineVul-BigVul CDR 76% Chromium vs 0% Linux; all LLMs higher CDR on Linux; best per-CWE PACC 18.18% (CWE-472) on small cells | 13, 14 | V | weak (small cells) |
| RQ2 | Prompting effects are model- and metric-dependent: few-shot helps only Mistral; CoT raises Qwen2.5 valid-only F1 but lowers PACC | 13 | V | weak |
| RQ5 | Temporal separation by release date cannot exclude LLM training contamination; unrelated-function labels carry residual noise | 17 | A | moderate |

## 14. Key quotes
> "When evaluated on VentiVul, performance drops sharply, with most models failing to detect vulnerabilities reliably or distinguish vulnerable functions from their patched counterparts." (p. 1)

> "All conservative F1-scores remain below 5.5%, and all PACC values remain below 6%." (p. 13)

> "This manuscript has been accepted for publication in the Journal of Systems and Software." (p. 1)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: all 20 PDF pages read, including references. Figures 3–7 (t-SNE plots, per-project and per-CWE bar charts, pp. 10–16) are images. Their key numbers were taken from the results text, which quotes them; we did not read bar heights.
- Venue status [I]: `venue_kind: preprint` (arXiv 2512.10485v4, 4 Nov 2026, p. 1). The PDF footnote states acceptance at Journal of Systems and Software (p. 1), but no JSS DOI/version was found in metadata. Treat it as "not peer-reviewed (author-reported JSS acceptance)" until a published version is added via `rlab add`. If the published version appears, it should replace this one.
- Metadata mismatch [I]: `metadata.json` `added_reason` mentions "RQ2 label quality vs family (WordPress PHP)" and "G6 cost/energy at realistic prevalence". This paper contains no PHP/WordPress data and no cost or energy measurement (C/C++ only, p. 3, p. 4; no cost reporting found by grep). Those motivations apply to a different paper; this one supports G2 (temporal OOD DL vs LLM) only.
- Uncertainties: the exact number of vulnerable functions in the Whole-File set (we assume 263, one per pair). Train/test split ratios for the four benchmarks are not reported. ReVeal's VentiVul coverage (functions dropped by preprocessing) is not quantified.

## qin2026review · ready · full-text · relevance high
**Summary:** A single-author narrative review with 32 references (2019–2026). It sorts methods into lightweight code Transformers versus large LLMs, and its central argument is that benchmark gains are inflated by duplicates, label noise, random splits and temporal leakage. It recommends a workflow where SAST tools generate candidates, an LLM ranks and explains them, and a human confirms.

**The points you asked about:**
- **Protocol and corpus:** No search protocol, databases, screening, PRISMA, quality assessment or stated time window. The only inclusion rule is "directly analyze source code" (p. 4). The corpus is the 32-entry reference list, several of which are themselves surveys.
- **SAST coverage:** Explicitly out of scope ("does not provide a separate review of traditional detection methods", p. 4). It still concludes that LLMs and SAST complement each other (p. 12), but cites only two references for this ([1] and Gnieciak [15]) and gives no numbers.
- **Hybrids:** Covered only conceptually (pp. 8, 13). The evidence cited is GRACE, DLAP and one context-enhancement study. None of the SAST+LLM detection or alarm-filtering studies we have are included (IRIS, RepoAudit, du2026reducing, xiong2026sifting, li2026llm).
- **Contradictions explained by evaluation setup:** Only in general terms. Table 2 is a risk matrix (pp. 10–11), and there is one worked example, a re-reading of PrimeVul Table V (p. 12). There is no study-by-study mapping of conflicting results to their setups. Its PrimeVul numbers match our ding2025vulnerability analysis.
- **Venue concerns:** Zeus Press journal (p. 1). The PDF has no received/accepted dates and no peer-review statement. OpenAlex lists no host organisation and shows it as not in DOAJ and not core; publication date 2026-10-29, cited_by 0. The text is inconsistent: three research questions in the introduction, four in §3.1, and an undefined "C2" (p. 12). I advise weighting it like grey literature and citing it for positioning only. I did not confirm that the venue is predatory.

**Evidence rows:**
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ2 | Gains inflated by duplicates, label noise, random/temporal splits, model-version changes; random-split F1 = "within-benchmark performance" | 1, 10 | A | weak |
| RQ2 | PrimeVul Table V re-read: F1 62.88–68.26% (BigVul) vs 1.91–5.82% (BigVul→PrimeVul) vs 18.05–21.43% (PrimeVul→PrimeVul) | 12 | A | moderate |
| RQ2 | GRACE/DLAP/context enhancement/M2CVD cannot be ranked because datasets, models and protocols differ | 12 | A | weak |
| RQ1 | SAST more stable within its rules, LLMs better at explanation; complementarity, not replacement (no numbers) | 12 | A | weak |
| RQ3 | SAST candidates → LLM ranking/explanation → human confirmation; judge by audit time and false negatives, not F1 | 8, 13 | A | weak |
| RQ3 | Cost items listed (API, GPU memory, latency, version drift, prompt maintenance); none quantified | 9, 12 | A | weak |
| RQ5 | Out-of-time + project-isolated tests, data cards, calibration, recall at a fixed false-positive budget, explanation verification, audit-time studies | 13 | A | weak |

## lu2025lab · ready · full-text · relevance high
**Summary:** Four DL detectors were trained on Juliet, Devign, BigVul and ICVul, then ReVeal and LineVul were tested on VentiVul, a new set of Linux and Chromium CVEs disclosed from 2025-05-01 (200 CVEs, 263 vulnerable/patched function pairs, about 2% vulnerable). Four open-weight LLMs were tested on the same data without fine-tuning. In-distribution DL F1 of 91–94.5 collapses to 3.47–8.65, and the LLMs reach 0.79–5.36 conservative F1, with patch-pair accuracy under 6% for every model.

**Venue status:** arXiv v4 (4 Nov 2026), whose footnote says "accepted for publication in the Journal of Systems and Software" (p. 1). There is no JSS DOI in metadata, so I flagged it as "not peer-reviewed (author-reported JSS acceptance)".

**DL vs LLM, in-distribution vs temporally separated:**
- **DL in-distribution:**
  - LineVul F1 94.52 and VulBERTa 94.14 on Juliet; LineVul 91.00 on BigVul (pp. 11–12).
  - On BigVul, ReVeal/Devign/VulBERTa reach accuracy 87.45/94.09/94.39 but F1 only 23.58/16.90/0.19 (p. 11).
- **DL cross-dataset:** LineVul trained on BigVul scores 0 / 1.90 / 13.05 on the other three datasets (p. 12).
- **DL on VentiVul:**
  - F1 3.47–8.65; best is ReVeal trained on BigVul at 8.65 (precision 5.25, recall 24.43). LineVul trained on BigVul gets 6.87 (p. 13).
  - Patch-pair accuracy (PACC) is under 5.5% for all DL models; best 5.34 (p. 13).
- **LLMs:** only evaluated on VentiVul, so there are no in-distribution LLM numbers. LLM precision and recall are not reported.
  - Zero-shot conservative F1: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B 3.72, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite 4.29, Qwen3-30B 3.09, Mistral-24B 4.07.
  - Best overall is Mistral few-shot: F1 5.36, CVE detection rate 46%, PACC 5.75.
  - Highest valid-only F1 is Qwen2.5 with chain-of-thought at 8.21 (3.04 conservative) (p. 14).

**Evidence rows:**
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ2 | DL in-distribution F1 high (94.52/94.14 Juliet, 91.00 BigVul) but drops cross-dataset (LineVul-BigVul → 0/1.90/13.05) | 11, 12 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Accuracy hides failure at 6% prevalence: BigVul accuracy 87–94 with F1 23.58/16.90/0.19 | 11 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | On VentiVul (~2% prevalence), trained DL F1 3.47–8.65 | 13 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | 4 open-weight LLMs on the same functions: conservative F1 0.79–5.36, PACC < 6%; zero-shot CVE detection rate 5–34%, below most DL configs | 13, 14 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | Both families are near an all-positive baseline (F1 ≈ 3.9%) | 4, 13 | I | moderate |
| RQ2 | CVE detection rate 94.59–100% with PACC 0–0.76% for Devign/ICVul-trained models; all DL PACC < 5.5% | 13 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | Project/CWE variance: LineVul-BigVul CVE detection 76% Chromium vs 0% Linux; best per-CWE PACC 18.18% on small cells | 13, 14 | V | weak |
| RQ2 | Prompting effects depend on model and metric (few-shot helps only Mistral; chain-of-thought lowers Qwen2.5 PACC) | 13 | V | weak |
| RQ5 | Separation by release date cannot rule out LLM contamination; "unrelated" functions may carry residual label noise | 17 | A | moderate |

## Surprising or doubtful
- **Results near chance:** The paper never compares its scores with a chance baseline. By my calculation (263/13,326 ≈ 2% vulnerable), an all-positive predictor scores F1 ≈ 3.9%. LineVul trained on Devign (recall 100, precision 2, F1 3.93) is effectively that predictor, and most LLM conservative F1 values fall at or below it.
- **Uneven DL vs LLM comparison:** The LLMs are mid-size open-weight models (two are mixture-of-experts with 2.4–3B active parameters), not fine-tuned, with Qwen3 thinking mode off. Inputs are single functions with no context. There are no SAST tools, no frontier LLMs and no cost figures.
- **Wrong reason recorded for adding lu2025lab:** The `added_reason` in its `metadata.json` cites "WordPress PHP" label quality and "G6 cost/energy". The paper is C/C++ only and reports no cost or energy, so that reason seems to belong to a different paper. I did not edit the metadata; the gap report should not use lu2025lab for G6 or the PHP point.
- **Qin as a competitor:** Its weak venue and lack of a protocol make it a manageable competitor. Our differences from it are a systematic method, SAST treated as a reviewed family, empirical hybrid evidence, and contradictions mapped study by study to evaluation setup. It still needs to be cited.

## Sections not completed
None. The figures were images: Qin's Figures 1–2 I read from the PDF page images. For lu2025lab's Figures 3–7, numbers come from the results text, not from reading the bar charts.
